title: Mama’s Pickles Online
teaser: Dina had no money and no office. She had her mother’s recipe.
paragraphs: Dina is twenty-three. She finished university two years ago, but she cannot find a job. Every day, she sends her CV to companies, and every day nobody answers.

Her mother makes the best pickles in their building in Faisal. Neighbours always ask for a jar. One evening, Dina has an idea. “Why don’t we sell them online?” Her mother laughs. “Who will buy pickles from Instagram?”

Dina starts small. She takes nice photos of the jars on the balcony in the morning light. She creates a page called Mama’s Pickles. She writes the price and the delivery areas. In the first week, she gets three orders. All of them are from her cousins.

But the cousins tell their friends. In the second month, Dina has forty orders a week. She learns to calculate her costs: vegetables, jars, labels and delivery. She realises she was selling too cheap, so she raises the price a little. Nobody complains.

After one year, Dina rents a small kitchen and hires two women from the neighbourhood. Her mother is the boss of the recipe. Dina still gets emails from companies sometimes. Now she does not need to answer them.

a request to buy something
bringing things to someone’s house
to find a number using maths
to pay money to use a place

recap: Unable to find a job, Dina sells her mother’s pickles online; it grows from cousins to forty orders a week and a small kitchen with staff.

title: Revenue Is Not Profit
teaser: The most common mistake new business owners make.
paragraphs: Imagine you sell 100 sandwiches a day at 30 pounds each. That is 3,000 pounds a day. Are you rich? Not necessarily. This number is your revenue: all the money that comes in. Profit is what is left after you pay for everything.
First, there are variable costs, which change with how much you sell: bread, meat, vegetables, packaging. If each sandwich costs 18 pounds to make, your variable costs are 1,800 pounds a day.

Then there are fixed costs, which you pay even if you sell nothing: rent, salaries, electricity, internet and the loan for your equipment. Imagine these are 25,000 pounds a month, or about 830 pounds a day.
Now the real picture: 3,000 − 1,800 − 830 = 370 pounds of profit a day. Still positive, but much smaller than 3,000. And if you sell only 60 sandwiches on a slow day, you may lose money.

This is why business owners calculate their break-even point: the number of sales needed to cover all costs. Every sale above it brings profit. Many small businesses close not because nobody buys from them, but because the owners looked at revenue instead of profit and spent money they did not really have.

targets.en: all the money a business receives from sales
money left after paying all costs
able to change
the boxes or bags things are sold in
money you borrow and must pay back
to be enough to pay for something

questions.q: What is revenue?
options: All the money that comes in

questions.q: Which is a fixed cost?
What is the profit per day in the example?
What is the break-even point?
options: The sales needed to cover all costs

recap: Revenue is all money in; profit is what remains after variable and fixed costs; knowing the break-even point keeps businesses alive.

title: Five Envelopes
teaser: Ahmed’s salary disappeared every month. His aunt had an old trick.
paragraphs: Ahmed works in a call centre in Maadi. Every month, he gets his salary on the first day. By the twentieth day, his wallet is always empty. He does not understand where the money goes.
His aunt, Tant Samia, worked in a bank for thirty years. When Ahmed asks her for help, she gives him five envelopes and a pen. “Write on them,” she says. “Rent. Food. Transport. Fun. Savings.”

On payday, Ahmed takes out his salary in cash and divides it into the envelopes. When the Fun envelope is empty, there is no more fun that month. He cannot take money from the Food envelope for new trainers.

The first month is hard. On day twelve, the Fun envelope is already empty, and his friends invite him to a concert. He says no and feels sad. But on day thirty, he still has money in the Food envelope for the first time in his life.

After six months, the Savings envelope is thick. Ahmed uses it to take an online course, and later he gets a better job. He visits Tant Samia with a box of sweets. “Your envelopes changed my life,” he says. She smiles. “No, you did. The envelopes just helped you see.”

a small case for money and cards
a paper cover for letters or money
money you keep for the future

options: His money finishes before the month ends

recap: Ahmed’s aunt teaches him to split his salary into five envelopes; he learns control, saves, takes a course and gets a better job.

title: Why Things Get More Expensive Every Year
teaser: Inflation explained with a plate of koshary.
paragraphs: If your parents tell you that a plate of koshary used to cost a pound or two, they are not exaggerating. The price of most things goes up over time. Economists call this inflation, and it means that the same amount of money buys less than before.

Inflation happens for several reasons. Sometimes demand grows faster than supply: if many people want to buy something and there is not enough, sellers raise prices. Sometimes costs increase: if fuel becomes more expensive, transporting food costs more, and shops pass that cost to customers.

The value of a currency also matters. If a country’s currency becomes weaker compared with the dollar, imported goods such as phones, medicine and wheat cost more in local money. Since many products contain imported parts, prices rise across the economy.

Central banks try to keep inflation under control, often by raising interest rates. Higher rates make borrowing more expensive and saving more attractive, so people and companies spend less, which can slow price increases.

For ordinary people, the most important lesson is that money kept at home loses value over time. That is why people try to save in ways that grow, such as bank savings accounts or investments, and why salaries need to increase just to keep the same standard of living.

recap: Inflation raises prices because of demand, costs and weaker currencies; central banks raise interest rates; money kept at home loses value.

title: Five in the Morning
teaser: Mai read that successful people wake up at five. She tried it.
paragraphs: Mai is a student in Assiut. She watches a lot of motivation videos. One video says, “Successful people wake up at five in the morning.” Mai decides to try it.

On Monday, her alarm rings at five. It is dark and cold. She makes coffee, opens a book and falls asleep on page two. On Tuesday, she does not hear the alarm. On Wednesday, she wakes up at five but feels terrible all day and shouts at her little brother.

Mai feels like a failure. She calls her older cousin, Heba, who is a doctor. Heba listens and laughs kindly. “Mai, what time do you go to sleep?” Mai answers, “About one o’clock.” Heba says, “So you are sleeping four hours. That is not a habit. That is a punishment.”

Heba gives her a different idea. “Don’t copy someone else’s morning. Choose one small habit and attach it to something you already do.” So Mai decides: after she drinks her morning tea, she will read ten pages. Any time. No alarm at five.
Three months later, Mai has read six books. She still wakes up at eight. She still loves motivation videos, but now she watches them with a smile and a question: does this fit my life?

a clock or phone sound that wakes you
a person or thing that does not succeed
something you do regularly

options: Successful people wake up at five

options: Attach one small habit to something you already do

questions.q: What is a “habit”?

recap: Mai fails at the 5 a.m. routine; her doctor cousin explains sleep and suggests attaching one small habit to her tea, and Mai reads six books.

title: How a Habit Is Built in Your Brain
teaser: Cue, routine, reward — and why motivation is not enough.
paragraphs: Most of what we do every day is not decided consciously. Researchers estimate that a large part of our daily behaviour is habit: brushing our teeth, checking our phone, the way we drive to work. Habits save the brain energy, so it can think about other things.

A habit usually has three parts. First, a cue: a trigger such as a time, a place, a feeling or another action. Then the routine: the behaviour itself. Finally, the reward: something pleasant that tells the brain this loop is worth remembering. Over time, the brain starts to expect the reward as soon as it notices the cue.

This explains why motivation alone often fails. Motivation goes up and down, but a strong cue works even when you are tired. If you want to study English daily, connecting it to an existing cue, like “after I pray Maghrib” or “when I sit on the metro”, is more reliable than waiting until you feel like it.

It also helps to make the new habit very small at the beginning, such as two minutes of reading. The goal is to repeat it until it becomes automatic; you can make it bigger later. Making the habit easy and visible, for example leaving your book on your pillow, reduces the effort needed to start.

Breaking a bad habit works in reverse: remove the cue, make the routine harder, or replace it with a better routine that gives a similar reward. For example, if you scroll on your phone when bored, keep the phone in another room and keep a book nearby instead.

targets.en: knowing and deciding what you do
the way someone acts
something that starts an action or feeling
nice and enjoyable
that you can trust to work
easy to see

questions.q: What are the three parts of a habit?
Why does motivation alone often fail?
How should a new habit start?
How can you break a bad habit?
options: Remove the cue or replace the routine

recap: Habits are cue–routine–reward loops; tying small new habits to existing cues beats motivation, and bad habits break by removing or replacing cues.

title: The Night Before the Exam
teaser: Mohamed planned to study all night. His sister had a better plan.
paragraphs: Mohamed has a big biology exam tomorrow. He has not studied much this month. Tonight, he has a plan: coffee, energy drinks, and studying all night until the morning.
At ten o’clock, his older sister Nada comes into his room. She is studying medicine, so she knows a lot about exams. She sees the three energy drinks on his desk and shakes her head.

“Your brain saves what you learn while you sleep,” she says. “If you don’t sleep, you will forget half of it tomorrow.” Mohamed is worried. “But I don’t know anything!” Nada sits down. “Then let’s be smart.”

She shows him a method. First, he reads one page. Then he closes the book and writes everything he remembers on a blank paper. Then he checks what he missed. “Testing yourself is better than reading again and again,” she says. They do this with the most important chapters until midnight.

Mohamed sleeps for seven hours. In the exam, some questions are hard, but he remembers many answers from his blank papers. He does not get a perfect score, but he passes with a good mark. That evening, he gives Nada his unopened energy drinks as a thank-you gift.

recap: Instead of studying all night, Mohamed follows his sister’s method of testing himself and sleeping; he passes with a good mark.

title: Why Cramming Fails and Spacing Works
teaser: The forgetting curve, and how to beat it.
paragraphs: In the 1880s, a German psychologist named Hermann Ebbinghaus did a strange experiment on himself. He memorised lists of meaningless syllables and tested how many he still remembered after hours and days. The result became famous as the forgetting curve: we forget most new information very quickly, often within a day, unless we review it.

But Ebbinghaus also found something hopeful. Each time he reviewed the material, he forgot it more slowly. The memory became stronger and lasted longer. This is the basic idea behind spaced repetition: reviewing information at increasing intervals, for example after one day, then three days, then a week, then a month.

Cramming, or studying everything the night before an exam, can work for the next morning, but the information disappears soon after. Spaced study takes the same total time but produces memories that last for months.

Another powerful idea is retrieval practice. Trying to remember an answer, rather than simply rereading notes, strengthens memory much more. That is why flashcards work well: they force you to recall the answer before you see it. Making mistakes during this process is not a problem; struggling a little actually helps.

Modern flashcard apps combine both ideas. They show you a card just before you are likely to forget it, and they adjust the timing based on how easy or hard it was for you. Ten minutes a day of this kind of review is often more effective than hours of last-minute studying.

the time between two events

questions.q: What is the forgetting curve?

recap: Ebbinghaus found the forgetting curve; spaced repetition and retrieval practice build lasting memories, unlike cramming.

title: The Lost Tourist
teaser: Youssef studied English for ten years. Today he finally has to speak it.
paragraphs: Youssef studied English at school for ten years. He knows the grammar rules and many words. But he has never spoken English with a real person. Every time he thinks about it, he feels afraid of making mistakes.

One afternoon in Khan el-Khalili, he sees a tourist looking at a map. She looks lost and tired. Nobody is helping her. Youssef’s heart starts to beat fast. He wants to help, but his English is “not ready”.

He walks past her. Then he stops, turns around and walks back. “Excuse me,” he says. “Can I help you?” His voice is quiet. The woman smiles. “Yes, please! I’m looking for the mosque with the tall minaret.”

Youssef forgets some words. He uses his hands a lot. He says “go straight” and “turn left” and makes a mistake with “on” and “in”. But the woman understands everything. They walk together for five minutes, and she asks him about his life.

When they arrive, she thanks him warmly. “Your English is very good,” she says. Youssef walks home smiling. He realises something important: people do not need perfect English. They need someone who is brave enough to talk.

title: Why You Learn More from Stories Than from Rules
teaser: The idea behind this app: comprehensible input.
paragraphs: For many years, language learning meant memorising grammar tables and vocabulary lists. Yet many students who did this for years still cannot follow a film or a conversation. In the 1980s, a linguist named Stephen Krashen offered an explanation that changed how many teachers think.

Krashen argued that we acquire a language mainly by understanding messages, not by studying rules. He called this comprehensible input: language that we can understand, even if it contains a few words or structures we do not know yet. Our brain picks up the new parts from context, the same way children learn their first language.

The key is the level. If a text is too easy, there is nothing new to learn. If it is too difficult, we understand nothing and give up. The ideal is slightly above our current level, which Krashen described as i+1. Research on reading suggests that we need to know about 95 to 98 percent of the words to understand a text comfortably and guess the rest.

Krashen also talked about the affective filter: when we are stressed, bored or afraid of mistakes, our brain absorbs less. This is why reading or listening to things we genuinely enjoy is so powerful. A football fan learns faster from football stories than from a textbook about shopping.

That does not mean grammar is useless. Knowing rules can help you notice patterns and correct your writing. But the bulk of your progress comes from huge amounts of interesting, understandable English. Every story in this app is written with that idea in mind.

targets.en: a person who studies languages

recap: Krashen argued we acquire languages through comprehensible input just above our level (i+1) when relaxed; grammar helps but input drives progress.

title: The Book Exchange
teaser: Sara had fifty books and no money for more. So she built a shelf.
paragraphs: Sara loves reading, but books are expensive. She has read all fifty books in her room three times. Her friends have books too, but they are on their shelves, and nobody reads them.

One day, Sara has an idea. She asks the owner of the café near her university in Zagazig, “Can I put a small shelf here? People can leave a book and take a book. For free.” The owner thinks for a moment. “If it brings more customers, why not?”

Sara puts twenty of her books on the shelf with a sign: “Take a book. Leave a book.” For the first week, nothing happens. Then one book disappears, and a new one appears: a novel in English with a note inside. “Thank you for this idea,” it says.

Slowly, the shelf gets busier. Students bring old textbooks. An old man brings poetry books from the 1970s. A girl leaves a comic and writes, “My first book in English. I finished it!” Some people start to meet at the café to talk about what they read.

Now there are three shelves, and the café owner is very happy. Sara has read forty new books this year, and none of them cost her anything. Her favourite part is the notes people leave inside the books.

title: What Fiction Does to Your Brain
teaser: Stories are not just entertainment. They may train empathy.
paragraphs: Reading a novel can seem like a way to escape from real life. But researchers who study reading suggest that fiction may also prepare us for real life, especially for understanding other people.

When we read a story, our brain does not simply process words. Brain scans show that reading about an action, such as kicking a ball or smelling coffee, activates some of the same areas we use when we really do those things. In a sense, we partly live the story.

Fiction also asks us to follow the thoughts and feelings of characters who are different from us. To understand why a character lies or makes a painful decision, we have to imagine their situation. Some studies have found that people who read a lot of fiction perform slightly better on tests of empathy, the ability to understand how others feel, although scientists still debate how strong this effect is.

Long-form reading also trains concentration. In a world full of short notifications, following a three-hundred-page story requires sustained attention. Many readers say that reading before sleep helps them disconnect from screens and relax.

For language learners, fiction has one more advantage: dialogue. Stories are full of the natural language people use when they argue, joke and apologise, which is often missing from textbooks. Graded readers, written at different levels, let learners enjoy all of this before they are ready for original novels.
